items.reason: No aired line, joke or device is near it. It mends the line before it (he is not quite on his own, he has a line he walks with) and brings nothing in. A host who walks alone is the character the ledger describes, and this is not a punch that he is only a host or is left out of something. Noted against the special and not against the record: it is the fourth time he says 'old' of a text, and the only one of the four that is not introduced.

Nothing aired quotes a poem, and no aired line has these words. Looked at against two things and passed. (1) The pilot's close, where the sincere thing was also said in borrowed words about friends (a real post held on a card as the answer to the night's question) and the host added a short line of his own. The subject returns, and so does the bible's own principle that the sincere words are someone else's; the device does not: no question is restated, nothing is on screen, it answers nothing that was asked, it is said to the road, and he then disowns it. (2) The two aired endings in which the house takes the host in. Nobody takes anybody in here: he lets slip that he was glad to be joined, and no one answers. Whether the quotation and its full stop match the card is the auditor's.

An idiom no aired line has. Looked at against what the two aired episodes did straight after their sincere moments: the pilot undercut its own with an animal call from the audience and a card, and the previous aired episode had the host make himself small ('I'm a mouth.') and then burp. Lightness within a beat of sincerity is the bible's craft and a writer may arrive at it; what is done is how each was staged, and neither is here. This line does not make him small or name what he is. It hands the feeling to the poem.

Looked at against the previous aired episode's 'Nothing gets in twice.' and then 'Except review.': a flat statement, a beat, and a short tag that takes part of it back. The figure is the same; the premise and the turn are not. There the exception was a fact the picture had planted (the word is in the pipeline twice) and the joke was one of logic. Here nothing catches him out: it is a concession of feeling, and it gives back half of what the line before withdrew. Like 'Same hour.' in round 2, it is a figure of ordinary speech used once; a third short walk-back as a beat of its own, in a later episode, would start to be a form. Within the special it is the second line of his own that he tops with a dry tag after a pause (`i-looked` is the first), three minutes apart and to the opposite effect.

joins: It joins cleanly at both ends, and it changes what the door is. In: after the crossing's last line there are 3.4 s of red and 5 s of snow with no words, and `this-block` is as it was. `one-line` grows out of it, so the poem needs none of the earlier draft's preface about a speaker walking alone: `this-block` has already said that, about Larry. No name has to be said and nothing is announced. The quotation is 1923 verse with two inversions and the word 'comrade', heard once; if a viewer does not parse it, the cue `glance` and the two lines after it still tell them that something warm was said and half taken back. The glance has a better reason than it had: it was a look at company and is now a man hearing himself. 'Mostly.' as a beat of its own, a step after the retraction, is better than the one line the earlier draft had. Out: about twelve seconds after 'Mostly.' he says 'There's an old Tamil book', with `this-is-me`, `started-without-me` and `q-come-up` between. Three things follow from that. Our staying on the pavement at the cue `listen-door` now has a cause, because he has just taken half of it back and we do not presume. `started-without-me` is now his second hedge in a row, about his friends this time, and it reads as the same man. And the couplet is now the second old text he gets behind in under half a minute, so the door is no longer where we first learn that he wants us to come; it is where he is caught at it again, with a whole book where he had one line. `position` is better for that, because the viewer is ahead of him. Further on, `company` gains: 'I had company.' is now the plain version, said to his friends, of what he could only say to us through a poem, and the writer was right to keep that word out of the block. Your closing line gains too: 'Keep the ones that make you feel sane close.' now has its old text behind it. Nothing later is broken by the four lines. For the sound editor, as the writer says, the steps under the block are about twelve seconds short.
earnsItsPlace: Yes. Not as a fourth piece of wisdom, which the special did not need, but as the one old text he keeps for himself. Taking the four questions in turn. (1) It still does what I praised at select, and it is leaner than it was there: the line is not his, he says it looking straight ahead, he glances and half takes it back, and the feeling is carried by where his head points. It has lost a hard name and a sentence of explanation and kept everything else. (2) The poem and the couplet do two jobs with one move. The poem is a feeling let slip and disowned, about what we gave him on the walk; the couplet is a reason for an act, about what he owes us at the door, and he pleads it. Neither uses the other's words. The move is the same both times, a warm thing said through an old text and then a dry line of his own to get out from under it, about a quarter of a minute apart. As written the first sets up the second: it teaches the viewer his tell, and the second is the bigger and funnier use of it. The cost is that the door was a discovery and is now a confirmation. (3) Four is not one too many, because this one is not a lesson: it is nine quoted words with no name, no date and no 'as I remember it', and it passes the cut test, since 'That's the poem talking.' and 'Mostly.' would be missed. What four does do is tip the piece: one old text in the first half, three inside about a hundred seconds of the second (the rabbi, the poem, the couplet). And it is about twelve seconds, which puts the special near 4:20 to black. (4) On the close. It does not add a fourth case of the house taking the host in: nobody answers him on the block. It runs the other way, and that helps: before the house counts him in and gives us a chair, he has let us know that he was the one glad to be joined, so we reach the table as his company and not as someone rescued from the pavement. But it adds one more sounding of the same warmth to a last two minutes that already had several: the poem, the couplet, 'Nobody has started.', 'I had company.', 'Chair.', the guest served first, and your own closing line. Each is dry on its surface, which is what keeps them apart. Accumulation is the thing to listen for, and it is the way sincerity fails that the special's own rules name.
forTheOwner: My round 1 advice was for an either-or: keep the couplet at the door, because the block's glance already carried the feeling without the poem. With both in, I think the pair works, for the reasons under earnsItsPlace. What it costs is the door as the first moment we learn he wants us to come.

The place to listen is the quarter of a minute from 'Mostly.' to 'There's an old Tamil book'. To my reading the second old text is funnier for the first. If it plays instead as coyness (he has just said he was glad, so why will he not simply ask), it will be heard in the hold before `q-come-up` and in how soon the couplet starts.

Three old texts now fall inside about a hundred seconds of the walk's second half, where there were two, and he says 'old' of all four. The poem being one line with nothing around it is what keeps it from sounding like a list.

The line is the hardest for the ear after the rabbi's: 'Rich did I feel when a comrade I found', two inversions and an unusual word, heard once. The captions carry it under your ruling. Nothing is drawn for it and the poem's speaker is not named, which is what its research card asks.

Your ruling on religion was given for the rabbi ('Keep the rabbi'). This is a fourth text from a tradition that some people living now hold sacred. It is treated as the others are, and whether the ruling reaches it is yours and the auditor's to say, not mine.

'Mostly.' is the fifth or sixth short dry phrase Larry ends a thought on ('I looked.', 'Same hour.', 'Some nights.', 'Still sharp.'). It is his voice in this piece and I would not lose this one; it is also about where a rhythm starts to be noticed.
About twelve seconds longer, so near 4:20 to black against the four minutes first aimed at. You chose that with the fourth idea.
